blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A pool has 4 crews. Four jobs each need 2 crews for 3 weeks and are due at week 3. Every due week is added as a rule end <= due. What does CP-SAT return?

options.text: OPTIMAL, with two jobs finishing at week 6, 3 weeks after their due week
options.says: A rule end <= due cannot be broken by any schedule the solver returns; lateness exists only when the due week is in the objective.

options.text: INFEASIBLE, since 24 crew-weeks are needed and 12 exist by week 3
options.says: Right: 4 x 2 x 3 = 24 crew-weeks against 4 x 3 = 12, the same count as the lesson's 36 against 18.

options.text: OPTIMAL, with all four jobs running in weeks 0 to 2, 8 crews at once
options.says: Four jobs of 2 crews at once need 8 crews; the cumulative constraint caps the pool at 4.

options.text: FEASIBLE, with a schedule found before the search proves the best one
options.says: No schedule meets every rule, and CP-SAT proves it: the lesson's version returns INFEASIBLE.

origin.section: Due Weeks as Hard Rules Make the Season Infeasible

questions.stem: A job is due at week 10 and the schedule ends it at week 7. Its lateness variable is set with add_max_equality(late, [0, end - due]), and its weight in the objective is 5. What does this job add to the objective?

options.text: -15: a credit of 5 for each of its 3 early weeks
options.says: The 0 in the list floors the lateness at 0; a credit for early weeks is exactly what the floor prevents.

options.text: 15: a charge of 5 for each week off its due week
options.says: Lateness counts weeks after the due week only; an early finish is not a deviation the objective charges.

options.text: 5: a charge of 5 for the job being in the plan
options.says: The weight multiplies the weeks late, which are 0 here; being scheduled costs nothing by itself.

options.text: 0: an early job has no weeks late to charge for
options.says: Right: max(0, 7 - 10) = 0, so the job adds 5 x 0.

origin.section: Lateness Is max(0, end − due), and Its Weight Is the Risk Carried

questions.stem: For one season, a makespan model and a weighted-lateness model with the same rules both return OPTIMAL, and both schedules end at week 24. Before computing either schedule's risk, what can you say about it?

options.text: Both carry the same risk, as both are optimal schedules
options.says: Each is optimal for its own objective; the lesson's pair carries $1,038k and $360k.

options.text: The makespan schedule carries less, as it ends work sooner
options.says: Both end at week 24, and in the lesson the makespan schedule carries almost three times the risk.

options.text: The lateness schedule carries no more than the makespan one
options.says: Right: the makespan schedule keeps every rule, and OPTIMAL means no schedule keeping every rule carries less risk than the lateness one.

options.text: Nothing can be said until a third model compares the two
options.says: Optimality of the lateness model already bounds every feasible schedule's risk, the makespan schedule's included.

origin.section: The Shortest Season Is Not the Safest One
